text: An Indicator of Compromise, or IOC, is a concrete, observable artifact that signals a system has likely been compromised — not a hunch, but something specific enough to match exactly. Today we'll walk through the four IOC types you'll run into constantly: file hashes, malicious IPs and domains, registry keys, and email patterns.

A file hash is a fingerprint of a known-malicious file's exact contents. A malicious IP or domain is a network address documented as attacker infrastructure, blockable at the firewall. A registry key is a persistence artifact malware plants so it survives a reboot. And an email pattern is a recurring subject line or spoofed sender from an active phishing campaign.

Here's why hashes are so reliable: the MD5 hash of the text "hello" is always the same thirty-two character string, on any machine, every single time, because a hash depends only on a file's exact contents. Change one byte and the hash changes completely. That's why EDR tools still catch a piece of malware even after it's renamed or moved to a different folder.

Domains work as IOCs too, and one of the most famous examples is the 2017 WannaCry ransomware. It checked whether one long, random-looking domain was already registered before encrypting a victim's files. A researcher registered it while investigating the sample, accidentally halting every future infection — an unintentional kill switch, and now one of the most documented network IOCs in security history.

Two more IOC types matter day to day. A registry Run key is a classic persistence artifact — malware adding itself so it launches automatically at startup. And a phishing campaign shows up as its own IOC: the same subject line hitting dozens of inboxes in an hour, or a sender display name that doesn't match the real sending domain. Every IOC here is specific and matchable, never a guess.

That's the four core IOC types — hashes, network addresses, registry keys, and email patterns — each one concrete enough for a machine to check automatically. Next up, Lesson 18 looks at how a SOC actually consumes a continuous feed of these indicators and turns them into automatic defenses.
